analysis.one_liner: Bans data brokers from selling or transferring people's health and location data.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the final weeks of the 118th Congress, sent to committee, and never received a hearing or vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for data brokers — companies that collect and resell information about people — to sell, license, or share a person's location data or health data, including data about pregnancies, mental health, disabilities, and medical care. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce the ban, and individuals could sue violators. Companies could face civil penalties of up to 15 percent of their parent company's annual revenue. The bill never advanced past its committee referral, and it died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone whose phone location, medical searches, pregnancy status, or health conditions could otherwise be packaged and sold — including people seeking abortion care, mental health treatment, or other services they may want kept private. The bill gives the FTC a dedicated $1 billion to enforce the ban.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone with a phone or health record

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it unlawful for a data broker to sell, resell, license, trade, transfer, share, or otherwise make available a person's location data or health data, whether the data was directly declared or inferred from other information [S2].
Health data is defined broadly to include searches for health services, disabilities, physical and mental health conditions, pregnancy and miscarriage, and treatments or diagnoses [S2].

Enforcement would rest on three tracks: the Federal Trade Commission could use its existing powers and also sue directly in federal court for injunctions, civil penalties, and damages; state attorneys general could sue on behalf of residents; and private individuals could sue for injunctions, damages, and attorney's fees [S2].

Violations would carry a civil penalty of up to 15 percent of the violator's ultimate parent entity's revenues from the preceding 12 months, and enforcement could require deletion of the improperly sold data [S2].
The bill appropriates $1 billion to the FTC, available through fiscal 2034, to carry out the work of enforcement [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers and the advertising and analytics companies that buy location and health data would lose a product line built on Americans' personal information. Companies would also bear compliance costs of building systems that wall off health and location data from sale.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers and ad analytics companies

drawbacks.text: The bill bans the sale and transfer of health and location data but does not ban collecting it, so data brokers could continue to gather and hold this information; it also carves out HIPAA-compliant actions, newsworthy publications, and disclosures the individual affirmatively authorizes [S2].

The definitions are broad — for example, 'location data' covers any data capable of determining a person's past or present location, and 'data' includes information merely 'reasonably linkable' to individuals or groups sharing a residence or IP address — which would require detailed FTC rulemaking within 180 days and could sweep in legitimate business practices [S2].

Critics of this style of legislation generally argue it raises compliance costs for firms and could chill ordinary digital services; the bill itself does not address those tradeoffs, and its penalty ceiling of 15 percent of parent-company revenue is a substantial exposure for large firms [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a hard ban on a market most consumers never knew existed: the routine sale of where they go and what their bodies are going through. The costs are real but ordinary for a data regulation — compliance costs and some definitional uncertainty — and the bill preserves the FTC's existing authority and includes carve-outs for authorized disclosures and journalism. The main design weakness is that it restricts sale and transfer without restricting collection, leaving the underlying data-gathering in place.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on December 19, 2024, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the same day, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever scheduled.

narrative.text: Representative Mary Gay Scanlon introduced the Health and Location Data Protection Act of 2024 in the House on December 19, 2024, with Representatives Jayapal, Velazquez, and Espaillat as the original cosponsors [S1] [S2].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day it was introduced; that was the last action recorded before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4] [S1].
The bill had three cosponsors in addition to its sponsor, all Democrats [S3].
Because bills do not carry over between Congresses, the bill's death on January 3, 2025 means any future attempt must start over with a new introduction.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers and the advertising and analytics companies that buy Americans' health and location data are better off, since the market for that data remains unrestricted. The committee also avoided taking a position, since no hearing or vote was ever held.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no roll-call split exists; the sponsor and all three cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill sat in a committee led by the Republican majority until the Congress ended [S3] [S4].

industries.note: These companies collect, infer, and resell Americans' location and health data; the bill would make that core business unlawful, with penalties up to 15 percent of parent-company revenue. Their interest in keeping the market open runs directly against consumers' privacy.

Ad networks and app analytics firms buy precise location and health signals from brokers to target ads; the ban would cut off that supply chain and force changes to how they monetize app and browsing data.

The bill explicitly preserves HIPAA-compliant handling of health information by covered entities and business associates, so normal medical-data operations are untouched while gray-market resale is banned.
